## Introduction: Neuroendocrine Tumors (NETs)

- NETs are a heterogeneous group of neoplasms originating from the diffuse neuroendocrine cell system
- Most commonly arise in the lung or gastrointestinal (GI) tract
- Although rare, NET incidence and prevalence continue to increase
- NETs are now the **second most prevalent GI cancer**
- Well-differentiated NETs are subdivided largely by tissue of origin
- **Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (PNETs)** originate from endocrine tissue of the pancreas (islets of Langerhans)

## Introduction: PNETs Overview

- PNETs are the **second most common tumor arising from the pancreas**
- Comprehensive diagnosis relies on:
  - Clinical symptoms
  - Imaging
  - Histopathology
- Management is challenging due to heterogeneity in:
  - Tumor behavior
  - Clinical presentation
- Approximately **30% of PNETs are functional tumors**
  - Produce clinical symptoms from hormone hypersecretion

## Introduction: Treatment Landscape

- Many advanced PNETs can be initially monitored due to indolent growth
- With time, disease will require treatment
- Decision to start therapy is driven by:
  - Increasing clinical symptoms (hormone secretion and/or tumor bulk)
  - High tumor burden
  - Progressive disease while on observation
- Treatment options are multidisciplinary:
  - Surgical resection
  - Liver-directed therapies
  - Systemic treatments

## Introduction: Metastatic PNETs

- For metastatic PNETs, treatment is **almost always noncurative**
- Survival can often be measured on the order of years
- Most patients will ultimately die of the disease
- This chapter reviews:
  - Classification
  - Clinical features
  - Diagnosis
  - Treatment of PNETs

## Epidemiology: Incidence

- PNETs account for approximately **7% of all NETs**
- PNETs account for **1% to 2% of pancreatic tumors**
- Incidence has risen over the past 30 years
  - From **0.17 to 0.43 cases per 100,000 people**
- Males and females are affected equally
- Most patients are diagnosed between ages **60 to 80 years**

## Epidemiology: Familial Predisposition

- Approximately **5% of patients** have an underlying familial syndrome predisposing to PNET development:
  - Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1)
  - Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL)
  - Tuberous sclerosis (TS)
  - Neurofibromatosis type I (NF1)
- These patients tend to be diagnosed at a younger age
- Family history significant for NET is the only well-established risk factor

## Epidemiology: Risk Factors

- Risk factors for pancreatic adenocarcinoma have **not** been associated with PNET development:
  - Cigarette smoking
  - Diabetes mellitus
  - Chronic pancreatitis
  - Obesity
- This distinction is important for understanding PNET etiology

## Molecular Biology: Overview

- Apart from germline syndromes, understanding of the genetic basis of sporadic PNETs has advanced in recent years
- Key pathways implicated:
  - Chromatin remodeling
  - DNA damage repair
  - mTOR pathway
  - Telomere maintenance

## Molecular Biology: Whole-Exome Sequencing

- One of the earliest studies performed whole-exome sequencing in **10 nonfamilial PNETs**
- Most commonly mutated genes were screened in an additional **58 PNET specimens**
- Increased number of mutations identified in:
  - Chromatin remodeling genes (**MEN1, DAXX, ATRX**)
  - mTOR pathway genes (**PTEN, TSC2, PIK3CA**)

## Molecular Biology: Whole-Genome Sequencing

- Whole-genome sequencing subsequently performed in **102 PNETs**
- Somatic point and gene fusion mutations observed in genes along four pathways:
  - Chromatin remodeling
  - DNA damage repair
  - mTOR
  - Telomere maintenance
- Larger than anticipated germline contribution identified
- Previously unreported germline mutations seen in DNA repair genes:
  - **MUTYH, CHEK2, BRCA2**

## Molecular Biology: Next-Generation Sequencing

- Benefit of NGS assessed in **96 tumor samples from 80 patients** with metastatic PNETs
- Somatic alterations identified in **95% of tested tumor samples**
- Most commonly altered genes:
  - **MEN1, DAXX, ATRX, TSC2**
- Sequencing of pre- and post-treatment samples revealed:
  - Progression in tumor grade
  - Clonal evolution in the tumors
- Germline analysis identified alterations in high-penetrance autosomal dominant cancer susceptibility genes:
  - **MEN1, TSC2, VHL**

## Molecular Biology: Poorly Differentiated PNECs

- Poorly differentiated pancreatic neuroendocrine carcinomas (PNECs) are clinically and genetically **distinct** from PNETs
- Most commonly mutated genes in PNECs:
  - Tumor suppressor **p53** (up to 95%)
  - Tumor suppressor **Rb** (74%)

## Pathology: General Features

- PNETs are generally **well-circumscribed, solitary masses**
- Can occur anywhere in the pancreas
- Majority of PNETs are well differentiated
- All PNETs have the potential to grow and eventually metastasize
- Because of this metastatic potential, these tumors are considered **malignant**

## Pathology: Malignancy Classification Criteria

- Because likelihood of metastatic spread is very low in some subsets, the term "benign" has been used as a classification variable
- Most classification schemes consider PNET malignant if it:
  - Invades locoregionally
  - Has metastasized distantly or to regional lymph nodes
  - Is greater than 2 cm in size
  - Displays vascular, lymphatic, or perineural invasion
  - Has a proliferative index greater than 2%

## Pathology: WHO 2017 Classification

- PNETs are classified according to the **2017 World Health Organization (WHO)** classification of pancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasms (PNENs)
- WHO 2017 criteria remain the **most significant prognostic tool** for clinicians
- Offers information to:
  - Predict tumor behavior
  - Guide selection of treatment
- Stratifies PNENs by:
  - Differentiation (well or poorly differentiated)
  - Grade (grade 1 low; grade 2 intermediate; grade 3 high)

## Pathology: Grading Parameters

- Grade is classified by proliferative index measured by:
  - **Ki-67** and/or
  - **Mitotic count**
- Mitotic index expressed as number of mitotic figures per 10 high-powered microscopic fields (HPFs)
- Recommended that **40 to 50 HPFs** be examined
- Ki-67 labeling tags neoplastic cells with an antibody and reports percentage of cells that stain positively

## Table 65.1: WHO Classification of Pancreatic NENs

| Terminology | Differentiation | Grade | Mitotic Rate (mitoses/2 mm²) | Ki-67 Index (%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| NET, G1 | Well differentiated | Low | <2 | <3 |
| NET, G2 | Well differentiated | Intermediate | 2 to 20 | 3 to 20 |
| NET, G3 | Well differentiated | High | >20 | >20 |
| NEC (small cell or non-small cell) | Poorly differentiated | High | >20 | >20 |

## Table 65.1: Key Points

- Well-differentiated NENs are defined as tumors (**NETs**)
- Poorly differentiated NENs are defined as carcinomas (**NECs**)
- The 2017 classification recognizes heterogeneity of grade 3 pancreatic NENs
  - Differentiates well-differentiated NETs and poorly differentiated NECs within grade 3 category as distinct subtypes
- Changes from 2010 to 2017 evolved through understanding of distinct treatment responses and clinical outcomes for grade 3 PNETs vs. PNECs

## Staging: AJCC System

- Most commonly used staging system in the United States is the **2017 American Joint Committee on Cancer tumor-node-metastasis system**
- Stage I: localized tumors
- Stages II and III: more advanced local or regional disease
- Stage IV: distant metastases

## Staging: 5-Year Overall Survival (SEER)

- 5-year OS rates (nonfunctional and functional tumors combined) derived from SEER database:
  - Localized tumors: **62%**
  - Regionally advanced disease: **54%**
  - Distant metastases: **20%**

## Prognosis: Overview

- Despite being classified as well differentiated, majority of PNETs have pathologic features that increase likelihood of future recurrence
- Many have metastatic disease at time of diagnosis
- Low- and intermediate-grade (G1 and G2) PNETs have significantly better 5-year OS than G3 tumors
- Functional tumors are associated with better survival than nonfunctional PNETs
  - More often identified at an earlier stage

## Prognosis: Survival by Grade

- 5-year OS by grade:
  - G1: **75%**
  - G2: **63%**
  - G3: **7%**
- Functional tumors vs. nonfunctional:
  - Functional: **68%** 5-year OS
  - Nonfunctional: **60%** 5-year OS

## Prognosis: Metastases and Age

- Approximately **60% of PNET cases have distant metastases at presentation**
  - Associated with decreased survival compared with local or locoregional disease
- Age at diagnosis helps stratify patients into prognostic categories:
  - Less than 55 years: **67.8%** 5-year OS
  - Greater than 75 years: **40.8%** 5-year OS

## Familial Syndromes: Overview

- PNETs are associated with four familial diseases:
  - MEN1
  - VHL
  - NF1
  - TS
- MEN1 is the most common of these syndromes
- Approximately **5% to 7% of patients with PNETs** will have MEN1

## Familial Syndromes: MEN1

- MEN1 is inherited in an **autosomal dominant** fashion
- Characterized by development of:
  - Parathyroid adenomas causing hyperparathyroidism in **90%** of patients
  - Multiple functional or nonfunctional PNETs in **75%**
  - Pituitary adenomas in **40%**
- Adrenocortical tumors (functional and nonfunctional), thymic tumors, and bronchial NETs also seen in some patients
- Genetic testing for MEN1 should be performed in all first-degree relatives (including children younger than 5 years) of affected patients
- Also for those who have had a germline mutation identified in the MEN1 gene
- Approximately **30% to 50% of patients present with metastases**
- Complications of metastases are the most common cause of death from MEN1
- Surgical management is complex

## Familial Syndromes: VHL

- VHL is an **autosomal dominant** syndrome caused by inactivation of the VHL gene
- VHL gene thought to play a role in angiogenesis
- VHL predisposes patients to several cancers:
  - Renal cell carcinoma
  - Pheochromocytoma
  - Cerebellar and spinal hemangioblastoma
  - Retinal angina
  - Endolymphatic sac neoplasms
  - Epididymal cystadenoma
  - Cystic and solid pancreatic neoplasms
- Between **10% and 15% of VHL patients** will develop PNETs
- Most common pancreatic manifestation of VHL is serous cystadenoma

## Familial Syndromes: TS and NF1

- PNETs may also develop in TS and NF1
- **Tuberous sclerosis complex 1/2 (TSC1/2)** inhibits mTOR
  - Defect in TSC2 gene leads to development of TS
- **NF1** gene regulates activity of TSC2
  - Loss of NF1 leads to constitutive mTOR activation
- In TS, hamartomas may develop in brain, eyes, heart, lungs, skin, kidneys, and pancreas
- In NF1, primary manifestation is benign neurofibromas in multiple locations of peripheral nervous system
- Patients also at risk for pheochromocytomas and sarcomas
- In both TS and NF1, multiple PNETs may develop in pancreas and duodenum

## Functional Tumors: Overview

- PNETs are clinically classified into two categories:
  - **Functional**
  - **Nonfunctional**
- Functional PNETs produce clinical syndromes because of hypersecretion of biologically active peptides
- Functional PNETs tend to have better 5-year OS compared with nonfunctional PNETs
- Likely because they are detected earlier due to presence of symptoms

## Insulinoma: Overview

- Insulinomas secrete insulin and/or proinsulin, causing **hypoglycemia**
- Represent **1% to 2% of all pancreatic tumors**
- Typically:
  - Small (less than 2 cm)
  - Solitary (except in MEN1)
  - Intrapancreatic
- In rare malignant cases:
  - 5-year OS is **56%**
  - 10-year OS declines to **29%**

## Insulinoma: Diagnosis

- Critical part of history is establishment of **Whipple's triad**:
  - Plasma glucose less than 40 mg/dL
  - Symptoms of hypoglycemia
  - Resolution of symptoms with a meal
- Diagnosis confirmed by drawing during a **72-hour fast**:
  - Plasma glucose
  - Insulin
  - C-peptide
  - Proinsulin levels
- This panel will detect **90% of insulinomas**
- Malignant insulinomas tend to produce higher levels of insulin and proinsulin
  - Thus more severe symptoms because metastases also secrete these hormones

## Insulinoma: Localization

- Most insulinomas identified with **CT or ultrasound (US)**
- When very small, these methods may not localize the tumor
- **Arterial stimulation venous sampling** may then be helpful
- Technique:
  - Right and left hepatic veins catheterized via femoral puncture
  - Calcium injected successively into gastroduodenal, proximal splenic, superior mesenteric, and proper hepatic arteries
  - After each injection, venous blood sampled from hepatic veins at 30, 60, and 120 seconds
  - Positive localization corresponds to a 2-fold increase in hepatic vein insulin levels
- Accuracy to localize tumor to a region of pancreas (head, body, tail) is **94% to 100%**

## Gastrinoma: Overview

- Gastrinomas secrete gastrin, causing **Zollinger-Ellison syndrome**
- Named for Zollinger and colleagues who, in 1955, published a case series detailing clinical courses of two patients with:
  - Gastric acid hypersecretion
  - Severe peptic ulceration
  - Pancreatic tumors
- Extraordinarily high levels of gastrin secreted by these tumors cause:
  - Recurrent peptic ulcers
  - Diarrhea
  - Reflux esophagitis
  - Thickened mucosal folds in the stomach (hallmark of disease)

## Gastrinoma: Etiology and Location

- These functional PNETs may be:
  - Sporadic (**67%**)
  - Familial (**33%**)
- Tend to be solitary tumors unless seen in context of MEN1
  - In MEN1: small, multiple, most likely found in duodenum (greater than 85%)
- Regardless of etiology, generally found within the **gastrinoma triangle**
- Majority of gastrinomas are considered malignant (**60%**)
- Have spread to regional lymph nodes by time of diagnosis
- Liver metastases often associated with gastrinomas that arise in the pancreas

## Figure 65.1: Gastrinoma Triangle

- Approximately **90% of gastrinomas** are thought to arise in this anatomic location
- The apex is at the junction of the cystic duct and common bile duct
- The inferior aspect lies at the junction of the second and third parts of the duodenum
- The medial extent lies at the junction of the head and body of the pancreas
- SMA, Superior mesenteric artery; SMV, superior mesenteric vein

## Gastrinoma: Diagnosis

- Laboratory diagnosis requires demonstration of:
  - Hypergastrinemia
  - Abnormal gastric acid secretion
- Can be done by obtaining:
  - Fasting serum gastrin
  - Gastric pH
- If gastrin level is **10 times normal** and gastric pH is **less than 2**, diagnosis is confirmed
- If results are equivocal, a **secretin or glucagon stimulation test** can be performed
  - Gastrinomas frequently express both receptors
  - Respond by secreting abnormally large amounts of gastrin to injected reagent

## Glucagonoma

- Glucagonomas secrete glucagon, causing **hyperglycemia**
- Extremely rare
- Only about **400 cases** reported in the literature
- Tend to be:
  - Large (greater than 6 cm)
  - Solitary pancreatic tumors
- Most common symptoms:
  - Glucose intolerance
  - Migratory necrolytic erythema
  - Weight loss
- Migratory rash is often the first manifestation
  - Starts in perineum and spreads to trunk and extremities
- Diagnosis: elevated plasma glucagon level with enhancing pancreatic mass on CT
- Approximately **60% have liver metastases at diagnosis**
- In a case report of 23 glucagonomas, 5-year OS (regardless of treatment) was nearly **75%**

## VIPoma: Overview

- Vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP)-secreting neuroendocrine tumors (VIPomas) secrete VIP
- Cause **severe secretory diarrhea**
- Tend to be solitary, intrapancreatic tumors
- Greater than **50% are metastatic at presentation**
- Hypersecretion of VIP (a neurotransmitter and intestinal secretagogue) leads to:
  - "Pancreatic cholera"
  - Also known as **Verner-Morrison syndrome**

## VIPoma: Clinical Features

- Characterized by:
  - Large-volume (average 4.5 L) watery diarrhea
  - Metabolic acidosis
  - Achlorhydria
  - Hypokalemia
- If not properly identified and treated, patients will eventually succumb to renal failure secondary to hypovolemia
- Diagnosis made by:
  - Radiographic evidence of a pancreatic tumor
  - History consistent with the syndrome
  - Demonstration of an elevated plasma VIP level

## Somatostatinoma

- Somatostatinomas (SSomas) have a **less-defined clinical syndrome** than other functional PNETs
- Not all tumors that hypersecrete somatostatin will cause symptoms
- Syndrome may include:
  - Glucose intolerance
  - Cholelithiasis
  - Weight loss
  - Diarrhea
  - Steatorrhea
  - Anemia
- Tumors may arise in pancreas (**56%**) or duodenum
- May be more aggressive if intrapancreatic
- Duodenal SSomas are associated with **NF1 in approximately 50% of cases**
  - If discovered in this context, less likely to be malignant

## Pancreatic Polypeptide-Secreting Neuroendocrine Tumors

- PNETs that predominantly secrete pancreatic polypeptide (PP) are extremely rare
- Whether they should be classified as functional is a matter of debate
  - No specific syndrome has been defined
- Patients may present with:
  - Intermittent abdominal pain
  - Pancreatitis
  - Some patients may develop glucose intolerance
- If these tumors occur in context of MEN1:
  - Tend to be multifocal and malignant
- PP can be used as a marker for PNETs in MEN1 patients
  - Fasting PP levels greater than three times normal correlate with presence of a PNET likely large enough to detect by standard imaging

## Nonfunctional Tumors: Overview

- Nonfunctional PNETs are characterized by their **lack of hormone production** and hormone-associated syndromes
- Have potential to produce peptides:
  - Pancreatic polypeptide
  - Chromogranin A
  - Ghrelin
  - Neurotensin
  - Subunits of chorionic gonadotropin
  - Neuron-specific enolase
- These peptides do not cause hormone-producing symptoms
- Patients that present with tumors classified as nonfunctional can develop symptoms of hormone secretion further into their disease course

## Nonfunctional Tumors: Proportion

- Difficult to know what proportion of PNETs are truly nonfunctional
- Reports vary widely, ranging from **10% to 91%**
- Wide range due to two main factors:
  - Rates calculated from single institutions may be lower because of referral bias for functional tumors at academic medical centers
  - Large public databases (SEER, NCDB) often identify higher numbers of nonfunctional tumors because they do not collect data on specific symptoms or hormone levels
- Default in these databases is categorization as nonfunctional unless a specific functional histology code is recorded
- Reasonable estimate of proportion of nonfunctional PNETs is approximately **75%**

## Nonfunctional Tumors: Presentation

- In one report, **39%** of these tumors were discovered because of symptoms related to the tumor's mass effect:
  - Abdominal pain
  - Jaundice
  - Weight loss
  - Abdominal mass
  - Nausea
  - Vomiting
  - Back pain
  - Pancreatitis
- Nonfunctional PNETs causing symptoms tend to be larger than those found incidentally (2.5 vs. 1.8 cm)
- More likely to have involved nodes at diagnosis

## Nonfunctional Tumors: Incidental Discovery

- Approximately **35% of PNETs are discovered incidentally**
- This is occurring with greater frequency as use of high-quality axial imaging increases
- In one series of incidentally discovered PNET:
  - 19% classified as having benign histopathologic findings
  - 52% had uncertain histology
  - 28% considered to have malignant pathologic features
- Benign tumors and those with uncertain histology were associated with 5-year OS of **89%** and **93%** respectively
- Malignant tumors had **50%** 5-year OS

## Biomarkers in PNETs

- Some blood biomarkers can be elevated in presence of a PNET:
  - Chromogranin A
  - Pancreastatin
  - Pancreatic polypeptide
  - Neuron specific enolase
  - Tachykinins
- However, there is a lack of laboratory standards
- Varying sensitivity and specificity in measuring these biomarkers
- Serum chromogranin A can be elevated in many conditions:
  - Kidney and/or heart disease
  - Proton-pump inhibitor usage
  - Other non-NEN tumors
- Currently no data justifying use of these biomarkers in isolation for diagnosis or treatment decision making

## Imaging: Overview

- Imaging and endoscopy are used for:
  - Primary tumor detection
  - Staging
  - Surgical planning
  - Evaluation of somatostatin receptor (SSTR) expression
- Modalities used most often:
  - CT
  - MRI
  - Endoscopic US (EUS)
  - Standard US
  - Somatostatin receptor scintigraphy (SRS)
  - Positron emission tomography (PET)

## Imaging: CT

- CT is often the **first modality** used to image PNETs
- Valuable for detection of primary, regional, and metastatic disease
- Sensitivity for tumors greater than 2 cm is **80% to 100%**
- More sensitive for hepatic metastases than for primary tumors
- Can detect some PNETs smaller than 0.5 cm
- More likely to miss small lesions when compared with EUS
- Should be obtained with oral and intravenous (IV) contrast
- IV contrast important because PNETs and their metastases tend to be **hypervascular** and best seen in arterial phase
- These lesions will wash out in venous and delayed phases
- Oral contrast helpful for visualizing the duodenum

## Figure 65.2: Contrast-Enhanced CT

- Arterial phase of a contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen
- Showing an early enhancing pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor in the head and uncinate process of the pancreas (white arrow)
- With a necrotic node medially (red arrow)

## Imaging: MRI

- MRI should be considered a **second-line test** for detection of primary PNETs
- Used when:
  - Superior delineation of hepatic metastases is required
  - Patients have an iodinated contrast allergy
  - Cases of renal failure
- Should also be obtained with IV contrast
- Tumors will be:
  - Hypointense on T1
  - Hyperintense on T2 images
- As with CT, lesions less than 1 cm may be missed, regardless of contrast administration

## Imaging: Ultrasound and EUS

- US is most commonly combined with endoscopy or used intraoperatively in localization of PNETs
- EUS may be used to:
  - Identify the primary tumor
  - Identify local nodal involvement
  - When combined with fine needle biopsy, obtain tissue diagnosis with diagnostic accuracy of **90%**
- EUS has a sensitivity of **79% to 82%**
- Can detect tumors as small as **2 to 3 mm**
- US commonly used intraoperatively to localize small tumors such as insulinomas
- In this role, sensitivity is **80% to 100%**
- Like EUS, highly operator dependent

## Imaging: Somatostatin Receptor Status

- Imaging is critical to clarify the SSTR status of the disease
- Scintigraphy with radiolabeled SST analogs has proven useful in diagnosis and treatment determination
- There are five types of somatostatin receptors (SSTR1 to SSTR5)
- **SSTR2** is frequently expressed on well-differentiated NETs
- Serves as primary receptor for both somatostatin analogue imaging and treatment

## Imaging: OctreoScan

- Original somatostatin analogue-based imaging modality is the **OctreoScan**
- Uses the radiotracer indium-111-DPTA-octreotide
- Produces a whole-body planar image with dark spots indicating where radiotracer has bound to SSTR2 (and to a lesser extent, SSTR5 and SSTR3)
- In most centers, planar images are enhanced by combining OctreoScan with **single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT)**
- SPECT adds axial three-dimensional imaging to the functional scintigraphic image
- Greatly improves diagnostic accuracy
- In one study, addition of SPECT to OctreoScan improved lesion detection by **52%**

## Imaging: 68Ga-PET/CT

- Most modern iteration of SSTR-based imaging combines PET with CT
- Uses positron emitter **gallium-68** to label various somatostatin analogues:
  - 68Ga-DOTA-Tyr(3)-octreotide (DOTATOC)
  - 68Ga-DOTA-1-NaI(3)-octreotide (DOTANOC)
  - 68Ga-DOTA-Tyr(3)-octreotate (DOTATATE)
- These bind to their respective SSTR subtypes
- 68Ga-PET/CT is the **preferred functional imaging of choice** over OctreoScan
- Each ligand varies in affinity for various SSTR subtypes, but differences are not clinically significant
- 68Ga-PET/CT will detect both functional and nonfunctional PNETs

## Imaging: 68Ga-PET/CT Performance

- Studies comparing 68Ga-PET/CT and conventional imaging modalities (CT, MRI, OctreoScan) consistently demonstrate **superiority of 68Ga-PET/CT** in detection of NET primary tumors and metastases
- Care must be taken to differentiate NETs from physiologic uptake of 68Ga, as is seen in:
  - Uncinate process of the pancreas
  - Pituitary
  - Spleen (or accessory spleen)
  - Kidneys
- Given its demonstrated utility in NET imaging, 68Ga-PET/CT was approved for general use in the United States in **2016**

## Imaging: 18FDG PET

- 18-Fluoro-deoxy-glucose PET (18FDG PET) is most often used in PNETs when the tumor is **high grade**
- Patients found to have PNETs with uptake on 18FDG PET are more likely to have early disease progression than those who are 18FDG PET negative

## Surgical Management: Overview

- Surgical excision of primary PNET, regional nodal disease, and distant metastases are required to achieve cure
- Cure is unlikely in the setting of distant metastases
- Despite this, patients may derive benefit from surgical resection in the setting of metastatic disease
- Should be evaluated and treated by a surgeon familiar with nuances of NET-directed operations
- In general, resection is indicated for:
  1. Functional, symptomatic PNETs
  2. Isolated G1 or G2 PNETs greater than 2 cm
  3. Patients with metastatic disease in which all visible metastases can be resected

## Surgical Management: Palliative Resection

- Palliative resection of the primary PNET and hepatic debulking may be considered for patients with symptomatic, advanced disease
- Where the liver is the only focus of distant metastases
- However, whether this affects overall survival is unknown

## Surgical Management: Small PNETs Debate

- It is generally accepted that nonfunctional PNETs greater than 2 cm should be resected, given their metastatic potential
- Much debate exists around what to do about smaller PNETs
- In many centers, these small tumors are observed with serial imaging and resected if they show signs of progression
- Evidence for this approach is conflicting

## Surgical Management: Lee et al. (2012)

- Compared patients with nonfunctional PNETs less than 4 cm:
  - Nonoperative management (n = 77; median tumor size 1 cm)
  - Resection (n = 56; median tumor size 1.8 cm)
- 9% of operative group had positive nodes; median tumor size 2.4 cm
- Mean follow-up 3.75 years (maximum 12.75 years)
- Median primary tumor size in nonoperative group did not change during follow-up
- No disease progression or disease-specific mortality in nonoperative group
- Suggests small PNETs can be safely managed nonoperatively

## Surgical Management: Sadot et al.

- Reviewed 464 incidentally discovered sporadic small (less than 3 cm) stage I to II PNETs
- 104 were recommended observation
- In observation group at last follow-up:
  - Median tumor size had not changed (1.2 cm, P = .7)
  - No patient developed evidence of metastases
- Within resection group:
  - Low-grade pathology recorded in 72 (95%) tumors
  - 5 (6%) developed recurrence after median of 5.1 years (range 2.9–8.1)
- No patient in either group died from disease
- Death from other causes occurred in 11 of 181 (6%) patients
- Authors concluded observation for stable, small, incidentally discovered PNETs is reasonable in selected patients

## Surgical Management: NCDB Study

- Study examining survival of patients in NCDB with localized, nonfunctioning PNETs less than 2 cm (n = 380)
- OS was significantly improved in patients who underwent resection of primary
  - Median survival greater than 5 years vs. 2.3 years in observation group
- However, because inclusion in NCDB requires a tissue diagnosis, this study would not have included many patients with incidentally found tumors being followed by imaging
- Therefore optimal management of nonfunctional tumors less than 2 cm is unclear
- In patients with significant comorbidities, it seems reasonable to observe these tumors
- Pancreas-directed operations are not without risk
- In Lee et al. series, 46% of surgically treated patients had some sort of perioperative complication
  - Most common was development of a pancreatic fistula

## Surgical Management: Procedures by Location

- Lesions in the body and tail are generally treated with **distal pancreatectomy**
- As larger tumors commonly invade the splenic vein, splenectomy is often performed
- In cases where tumors are small and do not invade the vein, splenic preservation should be considered
- Tumors in the head, especially if large, will require **pancreaticoduodenectomy (PD)**
- Small tumors in the head can be considered for **enucleation**

## Figure 65.3: Distal Pancreatectomy


- **A**, Intraoperative view of a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor located in the body of the pancreas
- **B**, Specimen resulting from distal pancreatectomy and splenectomy

## Surgical Management: Enucleation

- More limited procedures, such as enucleation, are acceptable for resection of small, isolated PNETs
- In well-selected patients, associated with relatively low rates of complications
- Three recent studies reported on safety and efficacy of enucleation for small (1–3 cm) PNETs
- Compared with patients who underwent PD or distal pancreatectomy:
  - Less blood loss
  - Shorter operative times
  - Fewer postoperative complications
  - Less pancreatic insufficiency
- Can be approached safely via laparotomy or laparoscopy
- Should be reserved for those PNETs most likely to be benign

## Surgical Management: Enucleation Criteria

- Generally performed on:
  - Insulinomas
  - Small, isolated gastrinomas
  - Nonfunctional PNETs
- Technical considerations:
  - PNETs should be 2 to 3 mm away from the main pancreatic duct
  - Less than 2 cm in size
  - Located relatively near the surface of the pancreatic parenchyma
- Intraoperative US should be used to help visualize location of the pancreatic duct during procedure

## Figure 65.4: Enucleation


- **A**, Enucleation of an insulinoma in the uncinate process
  - Tumor indicated by circle, with duodenum laterally (D)
  - Superior mesenteric vein pulled medially for exposure (arrow)
- **B**, Enucleation of a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor located at the superior aspect of the neck of the pancreas
  - Tumor (circle) is mostly detached at this point and rolled inferiorly over the pancreas
- GDA, Gastroduodenal artery; PV, portal vein; SV, splenic vein

## Surgical Management: Laparoscopic Distal Pancreatectomy

- To improve patient recovery, distal pancreatectomy may be performed laparoscopically or robotically
- Meta-analysis examined 18 studies including 1,814 patients with pancreatic tumors amenable to resection via distal pancreatectomy
- 43% underwent laparoscopic resection; rest approached with laparotomy
- Laparoscopic group had:
  - Shorter length of stay
  - Less blood loss
  - Fewer postoperative complications
- No difference in margin positivity, postoperative pancreatic fistula development, or mortality
- Trend toward fewer lymph nodes being sampled with laparoscopic approach

## Surgical Management: Primary Resection in Advanced Disease

- Common debate in management of NETs is whether to resect the primary tumor in presence of advanced disease
- One argument against resection: patient unlikely to obtain curative (R0) resection
  - Thus bears risk of large operation without potential benefit of improved survival
- Hill et al. (2009) compared patients with all stages of disease who underwent surgical resection with those who did not
- Found that those who had surgery had significantly better OS (median 114 months) compared with those medically managed (median 35 months)
- Trend persisted in subgroup with M1 disease
- Significant selection bias in such studies
- When primary is growing and/or thought to be at risk to cause complications such as bleeding, removing primary should be considered
- Alternatively, small primary that is asymptomatic and stable should be watched in setting of metastatic disease

## Figure 65.5: Surgical Resection and Survival


- Retrospective analysis of the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results database
- Hill and colleagues demonstrated that overall survival of pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor patients can be improved if surgical resection of the primary tumor can be performed
- Patients in whom surgery was recommended but not performed (including palliative procedures) had median survival on par with patients in whom surgery was not offered
- This observation held across all disease stages

## Surgical Considerations: Familial Syndromes (MEN1)

- Resection of primary tumor in context of MEN1 is more difficult and controversial than sporadic PNET
- Partial pancreatectomy will only treat tumor identified at time of operation
- Three types of PNETs most frequently encountered in MEN1:
  - Insulinomas
  - Gastrinomas
  - Nonfunctional tumors
- Imaging will frequently show multiple small tumors
- In many cases, both functional and nonfunctional PNETs will be present
- Resection of functional tumors is generally recommended

## Surgical Considerations: MEN1 Insulinomas

- Insulinomas typically arise in the tail of the pancreas
- When many PNETs are seen at time of surgery, some suggest a **distal pancreatectomy** (to level of superior mesenteric vein)
- PNETs in head of pancreas should be enucleated, if possible
- Cure rates of **90%** have been achieved with this method

## Surgical Considerations: MEN1 Gastrinomas

- Gastrinomas in MEN1 are more difficult to treat than insulinomas
- Much debate exists as to how to treat these tumors surgically
- Biochemical cure is rare and recurrence is frequent
- In MEN1, these tumors tend to occur in the duodenum
- In addition to careful US examination of the pancreas:
  - Transillumination of the duodenum
  - Duodenotomy for palpation of the wall
  - To ensure excision of all gastrinomas
- If number of gastrinomas in duodenum precludes simple excision:
  - Pancreas-preserving total duodenectomy should be considered
  - Along with enucleation of as many PNETs greater than 1 cm as possible
- More extensive surgery may be considered for primary gastrinomas greater than 2 cm
- If gastrinoma primary is in head of pancreas, especially if greater than 2 cm, a PD is indicated

## Surgical Considerations: VHL

- PNETs are found in **12% to 17% of patients with VHL**
- Approximately **17% of those tumors will eventually metastasize**
- Libutti et al. (1998) suggested PNETs greater than 3 cm should be resected
  - In their cohort, median size of PNETs in patients with metastatic disease was 5 cm vs. only 2 cm in those with localized disease
- Surgical strategy validated by prospective study:
  - 44 patients with VHL and PNETs observed or resected based on size
  - Followed for median of 32 months (range 4–110 months)
  - None that underwent resection developed metastatic disease
- Blansfield et al. (2007) suggested germline mutation in exon 3 and doubling time less than 500 days should also be considered
- Libutti study (2000) confirmed most patients with metastatic PNETs in VHL have mutation in exon 3
- No study has validated inclusion of Blansfield guidelines along with size criteria

## Management of Metastatic Disease: Lymph Nodes

- At least **20% of PNET patients** will have spread to regional lymph nodes at time of diagnosis
- No guideline on number of lymph nodes that should be sampled
- No requirement that formal lymphadenectomy be performed
- Lymph node metastases are associated with increased risk of recurrence
- Recent studies suggest a more aggressive approach may be of benefit

## Management of Metastatic Disease: Lymphadenectomy Study

- Bartsch et al. (2012) analyzed 48 cases of sporadic gastrinoma with N1 disease
- Patients had primary tumor resected (via variety of procedures) and systematic lymphadenectomy performed
- Included clearance of:
  - Peripancreatic and pancreaticoduodenal lymph nodes
  - Lymph nodes in hepatoduodenal ligament along hepatic artery
  - Lymph nodes between aorta and inferior vena cava
- To be classified as formal lymphadenectomy, more than 10 lymph nodes required to have been pathologically assessed
- Formal lymphadenectomy resulted in significantly higher postoperative biologic cure rate
  - Fasting gastrin less than 125 pg/mL and negative secretin stimulation test
- Trend toward improved disease-free survival
- In patients with sporadic gastrinomas treated by enucleation only vs. more extensive pancreatic procedure and formal lymphadenectomy, significant improvement in time-to-recurrence seen in those who had lymphadenectomy

## Management of Metastatic Disease: Hepatic Metastases

- Major consideration in surgical management of PNETs is how to treat hepatic metastases
- Seen in approximately **50% of patients**
- Curative resection is rarely achieved
- Surgical reduction of hepatic tumor burden may:
  - Diminish symptoms related to functional tumor syndromes
  - Delay liver failure secondary to hepatic replacement
- Surgical debulking of hepatic disease is appropriate for patients in whom estimated **90% reduction** of metastatic burden can be made
- Grade of tumor should be considered
- Debulking should be reserved for lower grade tumors

## Management of Metastatic Disease: Cytoreductive Techniques

- Gold-standard cytoreductive technique is **formal segmental resection**
- Other valuable techniques:
  - Wedge resection
  - Enucleation
  - Ablation (radiofrequency or microwave)
  - Embolization (hepatic artery embolization)
- These have advantages of preserving maximal amount of normal liver parenchyma
- Lower complication rates
- Ablative techniques best used for small volume isolated metastases (less than 5 cm)
- Because most patients with liver metastases have large, multiple tumors, hepatic artery embolic therapy is often most rational and preferred approach

## Management of Metastatic Disease: Transplant Criteria

- Standard set of criteria guide patient selection in patients with NETs
- Preoperative factors that may predict poor outcome:
  - Location of primary in pancreas or duodenum
  - Need for upper abdominal exenteration
  - Hepatomegaly
- Patient presenting for transplant with a PNET and hepatomegaly has estimated 5-year survival of **12%**
- Improves to **68%** if patient has only one or neither of those factors
- Transplant is rarely curative

## Nonsurgical Management: Indications

- Medical management for PNETs is indicated for patients with:
  - Clinical symptoms (hormone secretion and/or tumor bulk)
  - High tumor burden
  - Metastatic disease
  - High-grade disease (particularly nonlocalized)
  - Progressive disease
- In presence of metastases, treatment is almost always noncurative
- Goals should be to:
  - Improve quality of life
  - Extend survival

## Nonsurgical Management: Symptom Control

- Symptoms of insulinomas and gastrinomas can be treated with medications
- Hypoglycemia seen with insulinomas can be treated with **diazoxide** (200–600 mg/day)
  - Fast-acting drug
  - May only work in approximately 50% of patients
  - Nearly 50% of patients taking drug will experience side effects:
    - Fluid retention
    - Nausea
    - Hirsutism
    - Palpitations
    - Anorexia
- Symptoms secondary to Zollinger-Ellison syndrome are best treated with **proton-pump inhibitors (PPIs)**
  - Dose should be titrated to effect
- If patients are not candidates for surgery, they can be sustained on PPI over long term
- Studies show patients treated for more than 10 years do not develop tachyphylaxis
- May develop achlorhydria, which can lead to nutritional deficiencies

## Systemic Therapy: Overview

- Given heterogeneity of PNETs, systemic therapy strategy depends on several factors:
  - Tumor functional status
  - Pathologic grade of the tumor
  - SSTR avidity on functional imaging
  - Disease bulk
  - Disease behavior

## Systemic Therapy: Somatostatin Analogs

- Most well-differentiated NETs express SSTRs on their surface
- Most commonly subtype 2
- Are avid on functional imaging (OctreoScan or gallium-68 Dotatate PET/CT)
- Somatostatin analogs (SSAs; octreotide and lanreotide) are typically considered for **first-line treatment** of advanced and progressive SSTR-avid PNETs
- Can also be used to moderate symptoms in a number of functional PNETs
- SSAs mediate antiproliferative activity by binding primarily to SSTR2, SSTR5, and SSTR3
- Eventually stimulate cell-cycle arrest and inhibition of mitosis
- Well tolerated
- Most common side effects:
  - Flatulence
  - Diarrhea or steatorrhea
  - Nausea
  - Cholelithiasis
  - Glucose intolerance

## Systemic Therapy: PROMID Study

- Role for SSAs in cytostatic control demonstrated in PROMID and CLARINET studies
- PROMID study:
  - 85 patients with well-differentiated, functioning and nonfunctioning, metastatic midgut NETs
  - Randomized: 42 to receive octreotide long-acting-release (LAR), 43 to receive placebo intramuscularly monthly
  - Primary endpoint: progression-free survival (PFS)
- At 6 months:
  - 66.7% of octreotide recipients and 37.2% of placebo recipients had stable disease
  - Significant difference in median time to tumor progression (14.3 vs. 6 months, P less than .001)

## Systemic Therapy: CLARINET Study

- Similar benefit of prolonged PFS demonstrated with use of SSA lanreotide
- CLARINET study:
  - 204 patients with advanced, well- or moderately differentiated, nonfunctioning, low- or intermediate-grade NETs
  - Randomized: 101 receiving lanreotide, 103 receiving placebo monthly
- At 24 months:
  - 65.1% of lanreotide recipients and 33% of placebo recipients estimated to be progression free
  - Median PFS not reached vs. 18 months, P less than .001

## Systemic Therapy: NCCN Guidelines for SSAs

- Findings from PROMID and CLARINET illustrated clinically relevant antiproliferative effects of SSAs in patients with NETs
- National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines recommend use of either octreotide LAR or lanreotide in first-line for:
  - Relief of symptoms (in setting of hormone release)
  - Tumor control in patients with SSTR-avid NETs

## Systemic Therapy: Targeted Therapies Overview

- Targeted therapies sunitinib and everolimus have both demonstrated activity
- Both are approved for treatment of advanced PNETs
- Because of highly vascular nature of PNETs, inhibition of angiogenesis is a favorable target
- **Everolimus** is an mTOR inhibitor
- **Sunitinib** is a multitargeted receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor
  - Blocks vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)
  - Platelet-derived growth factor (PDGFR)
  - c-KIT

## Systemic Therapy: Everolimus and RADIANT-3

- mTOR pathway regulates cell survival, proliferation, and metabolism
- Several genes in pathway important in development of familial syndromes (NF1, TS)
- Efficacy of everolimus and its FDA approval for PNETs established through RADIANT-3
- RADIANT-3:
  - 410 patients with advanced and progressive PNETs randomly assigned
  - 207 patients received everolimus; 203 received placebo daily with best supportive care
- Treatment with everolimus associated with improved median PFS by 6.4 months (11 months vs. 4.6 months)
- Increased response rate (5% vs. 2%) compared with placebo
- Everolimus well tolerated
- Most adverse events grade 1 or 2 (stomatitis, rash, diarrhea, fatigue, upper respiratory infections)

## Systemic Therapy: Everolimus Survival Analysis

- In later survival analysis:
  - Patients randomly assigned to everolimus had median OS of **44 months**
  - Longest OS reported in a phase III study for this population
- Crossover from placebo to open-label everolimus allowed at disease progression
- 172 patients (85%) initially randomized to placebo did crossover to receive everolimus
- 37.7 month OS reported for placebo cohort

## Systemic Therapy: Everolimus in Insulinoma

- Important to note that everolimus can be effective in treating insulinomas
- One of drug's known side effects is induction of glucose intolerance
- This may eliminate symptoms of hypoglycemia in some patients
- Phase II study investigated synergistic effects of everolimus and octreotide in 50 NET patients
  - 14 of whom had PNETs
- Of PNETs:
  - 14% had partial response
  - None had complete response
- Although response rates were relatively poor, clinical benefit rate for this regimen was **92%**
  - Better than many other drug combinations

## Systemic Therapy: Sunitinib

- Sunitinib is an effective therapy for PNETs
- Efficacy demonstrated in a randomized, multinational, phase III study
- 171 patients with advanced and well-differentiated PNETs randomized to receive:
  - Best supportive care with addition of daily sunitinib
  - Placebo
- Study stopped early because:
  - Serious adverse events and deaths observed in placebo group
  - PFS favored sunitinib (median PFS 11.4 months vs. 5.5 months)
- Notable difference in objective overall response (9.3% in sunitinib arm vs. 0% in placebo arm)
- Findings led to FDA approval of sunitinib in PNETs
- In later survival analysis, five-year OS difference of 9.5 months confirmed for sunitinib arm vs. placebo arm

## Systemic Therapy: Cytotoxic Chemotherapy Overview

- Chemotherapy is typically reserved for PNET patients who have:
  - High-grade disease
  - Heavy tumor burden
  - Aggressive clinical course
- Role for chemotherapy examined in several single and combination-drug studies
- Evidence for survival benefit is conflicting
- Results demonstrate symptomatic and cytostatic benefits
- Previously investigated and commonly used chemotherapy agents include:
  - Alkylating agents
  - Platinum drugs

## Systemic Therapy: Alkylating Agents

- Alkylating agents investigated for PNET treatment include:
  - Streptozocin
  - Dacarbazine
  - Temozolomide
- Earliest evidence for use of alkylating drugs in PNETs comes from a case series describing patients with insulinoma treated with streptozocin
  - Saw relief in hormonal symptoms and cytostatic control
- Randomized study from Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) later demonstrated activity with streptozocin
- However, in ECOG study, streptozocin therapy associated with symptoms (nausea and vomiting) compromising quality of life and treatment compliance
- Follow-up retrospective efforts demonstrated mixed findings regarding role for treatment with streptozocin

## Systemic Therapy: Dacarbazine

- Dacarbazine first studied in carcinoid tumors
  - Tumor shrinkage and improvement in quality of life noted
- Role for dacarbazine in PNET treatment came from phase II ECOG study (E6282)
- Included 50 patients with advanced PNETs
- Observed response rate was **34%**
- Majority of responses occurred in chemo-naïve patients
- Median OS was **19.3 months**
- Notable lethal toxicities observed:
  - Septic shock
  - Myocardial infarctions
  - Multiple grade 4 hematologic adverse events
- Given potential adverse events, widespread use of dacarbazine has been limited

## Systemic Therapy: Temozolomide

- Temozolomide investigated as therapy for PNETs
- Effort to identify a less toxic alternative to dacarbazine
- Notable phase II data demonstrated role for:
  - Single-agent temozolomide
  - Temozolomide in combination with capecitabine (CAPETEM)
- For advanced PNET treatment
- Most notable toxicity with temozolomide is **myelosuppression**
- Blood counts must be carefully monitored during treatment

## Systemic Therapy: ECOG E2211

- Question regarding benefit of single vs. combination temozolomide therapy addressed in prospective ECOG E2211 study
- 144 PNET patients with advanced low or intermediate grade progressive disease enrolled
- Two-arm, phase II trial
- Randomized to receive temozolomide alone or CAPETEM
- Median PFS in temozolomide and CAPETEM arms:
  - 14.4 months and 22.7 months, respectively
- Median OS in temozolomide arm was 38 months
- Data review ongoing; OS for CAPETEM arm not yet reached
- Association noted between CAPETEM and improved PFS and OS compared with temozolomide alone

## Systemic Therapy: Platinum Agents

- Chemotherapy regimens incorporating cisplatin and carboplatin investigated as treatment options for PNETs
- Benefit may be limited largely to patients with higher grade tumors
- In largest retrospective study, 305 patients with advanced GI NENs included
- Study concluded tumors with Ki-67 less than 55% were less responsive to platinum-based chemotherapy
- Importantly, patients with tumors of Ki-67 less than 55% did still experience longer survival
- Highlights varying biology within high-grade cohort of NENs

## Systemic Therapy: Oxaliplatin-Based Regimens

- Two prospective phase II studies suggested antitumor activity in previously progressing NETs
- Based on radiographic responses and prolonged disease stability
- First study:
  - Evaluated oxaliplatin, leucovorin, and 5-flurouracil (FOLFOX) plus bevacizumab in progressing and advanced carcinoid, PNETs, and poorly differentiated NECs
  - After 12 treatment cycles, in 12 PNET patients eligible for response assessment:
    - Response rate 41.7% (5/12)
    - Median PFS 21 months
- Second study:
  - Evaluated 40 advanced NET patients treated with oxaliplatin and capecitabine plus bevacizumab for four cycles
  - Option to continue bevacizumab plus or minus capecitabine thereafter
  - Response rate 18%
  - Median PFS 16.7 months

## Systemic Therapy: PNECs Treatment

- PNECs are most commonly treated with a platinum drug (cisplatin or carboplatin) and etoposide
- These tumors are histologically like small-cell lung cancers
- Response rates vary from **42% to 67%**
- Median survival hovers just at more than 1 year
- Newer drug combinations have been suggested
- Response rates do not exceed those obtained with platinum and etoposide

## Peptide Receptor Radionuclide Therapy (PRRT): Overview

- PRRT targets and treats NETs with radiolabeled SSAs
- In PRRT, an SSA is linked to a therapeutic beta-emitting radioisotope via a chelator
- Allows for systemic delivery of targeted radiation to tumors
- When radiolabeled SSA binds to surface of tumor, targeted radiation is emitted
- Kills tumor cells as well as neighboring cells
- Given mechanism of action, SSTR expression on functional imaging is an important predictor of response to PRRT

## PRRT: Radionuclides

- First-generation radionuclide investigated for use in PRRT was a gamma-emitting **111Indium**
  - Short particle ranges
  - Weak therapeutic (cytotoxic) effects
- Next-generation radionuclides investigated were beta-emitting:
  - **90Yttrium (90Y)**
  - **177Lutetium (177Lu)**
- These increased particle ranges
- Killing neighboring tumor cells and improving cytotoxicity

## PRRT: Clinical Studies

- Role for PRRT in treatment of advanced PNETs demonstrated in several studies
- Most notable toxicities include:
  - Myelosuppression
  - Nephrotoxicity
- Most efforts have used 177Lu-based radiolabeled SSAs
- Results show benefit in:
  - Reduction of tumor size
  - Survival
  - Quality of life
- In a large study, 504 advanced NETs treated with four cycles of 177Lu-DOTATATE at 6- to 10-week intervals
  - Median OS of 46 months (128 months from diagnosis) from start of treatment
  - Increased survival benefit of 40 to 72 months from time of diagnosis compared with historical controls

## PRRT: Erasmus Medical Center Experience

- Largest retrospective effort reviewed outcomes of more than 1,200 patients treated at Erasmus Medical Center
- Received 177Lu-DOTATATE infusion for four treatments at 8-week intervals
- Objective response rate of **39%** observed
- 43% of patients achieved stable disease
- PFS and OS were 29 months and 63 months, respectively
- Long-term toxicities primarily hematologic:
  - Acute leukemia in 4 patients (0.7%)
  - Myelodysplastic syndrome in 9 patients (1.5%)

## PRRT: NETTER-1 Trial

- NETTER-1 was first prospective, randomized trial of PRRT
- 229 patients with progressive, well-differentiated metastatic midgut NETs randomized to receive:
  - 177Lu-DOTATATE plus octreotide LAR
  - Octreotide LAR alone
- At analysis, PFS at 20 months:
  - 65.2% in 177Lu-DOTATATE group
  - 10.8% in control group
- Observed overall response rate:
  - 18% in 177Lu-DOTATATE group
  - 3% in control group
- Fourteen deaths observed in 177Lu-DOTATATE group vs. 26 deaths in control group
- Grade 3/4 toxicities observed in 177Lu-DOTATATE group:
  - Neutropenia (1%)
  - Thrombocytopenia (2%)
  - Lymphopenia (9%)
- 177Lu-DOTATATE was FDA approved for treatment of advanced gastroenteropancreatic NETs in **2018**
  - Because of data reported from Erasmus Medical Center study and NETTER-1 trial

## Surveillance and Follow-Up: NCCN Guidelines

- NCCN has guidelines outlining surveillance and follow-up of PNETs
- If a patient has been resected:
  - Biochemical markers and contrast-enhanced CT or MRI can be obtained at least once in the 3 to 12 months after surgery, as clinically indicated
- Thereafter, if patient does not recur:
  - Followed every 6 to 12 months for 10 years
  - With examination, biochemical markers, and cross-sectional imaging as clinically indicated
- Exception: benign insulinoma
  - May only need to be followed for 1 to 2 years
  - Unless patient had multiple lesions or has MEN1

## Surveillance and Follow-Up: Recurrence or Advanced Disease

- If patient experiences a recurrence, has G3 disease, or has locoregional or distant unresectable disease:
  - Follow-up determined by patient's clinical condition and behavior of tumor
- Asymptomatic patient with low tumor burden:
  - Can be followed every 3 to 12 months with clinical examination and imaging
- Onset of new symptoms or evidence of disease progression should prompt more frequent follow-up

## Summary: Key Takeaways

- PNETs are rare but increasing in incidence
- Second most common tumor arising from the pancreas
- Approximately 30% are functional tumors
- Diagnosis relies on clinical symptoms, imaging, and histopathology
- WHO 2017 classification is the most significant prognostic tool
- Treatment is multidisciplinary:
  - Surgical resection
  - Liver-directed therapies
  - Systemic treatments
- For metastatic PNETs, treatment is almost always noncurative
- Most patients will die of the disease, though survival can be measured in years

## Summary: Therapeutic Landscape

- **Somatostatin analogs**: first-line for SSTR-avid advanced/progressive PNETs
- **Everolimus** (mTOR inhibitor): approved for advanced PNETs
- **Sunitinib** (TKI): approved for advanced PNETs
- **Cytotoxic chemotherapy**: reserved for high-grade, heavy tumor burden, or aggressive disease
- **PRRT** (177Lu-DOTATATE): approved for advanced gastroenteropancreatic NETs
- Surveillance with biochemical markers and cross-sectional imaging is essential
- Multidisciplinary care is critical for optimal outcomes
